# Stripping Factory Finishes from STI Calipers

Refinishing STI brake calipers requires a level of precision that mirrors careful code refactoring: you want to remove the legacy implementation without introducing bugs (corrosion or surface damage) into your new build. The factory finish on these units is typically an electrocoat base followed by a clear coat, designed for durability and heat resistance. Simply blasting them off with sandpaper often leaves micro-abrasions that prevent proper adhesion of your new paint system, leading to peeling after just a few thermal cycles.

The most reliable approach involves chemical stripping rather than mechanical abrasion. For the black finish found on 2014 STI calipers and similar Subaru components, a dedicated automotive paint stripper is necessary. Avoid using household solvents like acetone or generic rust removers; they are often insufficient to break down electrocoat layers and can leave oily residues that interfere with primer bonding.

A common workflow involves applying a thick layer of chemical stripper specifically rated for baked-on enamels and clear coats. Allow the product to dwell according to the manufacturer's instructions, usually 15 to 30 minutes, until the finish bubbles and lifts. Once softened, gently scrape the residue away using a plastic scraper or a wooden stick. Using metal scrapers at this stage is risky; even slight gouges in the bare aluminum will act as stress risers during braking, potentially causing cracks that propagate over time.

After removing the bulk of the paint, you must address the white lettering and any remaining stubborn spots. Here, mechanical methods become necessary but require extreme care. A Dremel tool fitted with a fine-grit sanding drum or a dedicated stripping wheel can remove lettering without damaging the underlying metal. The goal is to feather the edges where the old paint meets the bare metal, ensuring no sharp transition lines remain.

Once the surface is stripped, cleaning is non-negotiable. Any trace of stripper or oil will compromise the chemical bond of your primer. A wash with a dedicated degreaser like Simple Green or acetone, followed by a thorough wipe-down with brake cleaner and lint-free towels, ensures the substrate is chemically clean.

Finally, surface preparation dictates paint longevity. Even after stripping, calipers often have pitting from years of exposure to road salts and brake dust. Sanding the entire surface with 400-grit paper removes imperfections and creates a mechanical profile for the primer. Follow this with 600 or 800 grit to smooth out scratches before applying etching primer. Without proper priming, standard automotive paint will peel within months of aggressive braking.

The trade-off here is time versus quality. Mechanical stripping (sanding) is faster but carries a higher risk of uneven removal and subsurface damage. Chemical stripping is slower and requires ventilation but yields a smoother, more uniform canvas for your custom finish. If you are building a system where long-term reliability is critical, the extra hour spent on chemical stripping pays dividends in the longevity of the paint job.

For those interested in deeper discussions on automotive restoration techniques or sourcing specific industrial solvents, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) occasionally cover niche hardware topics, though they are not a primary source for mechanical repair guides. The focus here remains on the chemistry and physics of adhesion that ensure your custom calipers survive the rigors of track use or daily driving without failing prematurely.
